newsitem.title: USA: Singer Tammy Wynette battles tabloids in court.
newsitem.headline: Singer Tammy Wynette battles tabloids in court.

text.p: Lawyers for two supermarket tabloids -- the National Enquirer and the Star -- asked a federal court Monday to throw out a suit against them by country music's Tammy Wynette, insisting that "almost anything in a celebrity's life is of public interest."

Judge John Nixon of U.S. District Court heard attorneys for the "first lady of country music" claim her privacy was violated after both publications ran stories on her in 1995 when she was hospitalized in Pittsburgh.
Nixon took the case under advisement, promising "I'll get you a decision as soon as I can."

Wynette was not in court but her husband, George Richey, heard Gerson Zweifach, attorney for the National Enquirer, tell the judge that Wynette had undergone 14 major surgeries during 31 different hospitalizations over the past 25 years.
"She has had surgeries for everything under the sun," Zweifach said. "That would be newsworthy with a private individual, but we're talking about one of the most famous people in the world."

Nashville lawyer Gary Blackburn, presenting Wynette's case, said the publications paid an employee to give them information and would not identify their source. Both publications are owned by American Media, Inc.
Blackburn called the publications' conduct "truly outrageous."
"They have wrapped themselves in the flag and hidden behind the First Amendment," he said.
In addition to invasion of privacy, Wynette is suing for defamation, libel, misusing her name and likeness for commercial gain and interfering with potential business relationships.

Asked by the judge why defamation would be involved in disclosing medical records, Blackburn said it would affect Wynette's booking possibilities for concert dates. He also claimed the publications had described Wynette as in dire need of a liver transplant, which was untrue.
The judge agreed the medical records were confidential but questioned whether their publication was injurious to a reputation.
